vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits in the therapy office with his hands gripping the armrests of the chair. At thirty-nine, he carries himself with the precision you'd expect from someone trained to manage complex systems under pressure, yet there's a brittleness to his posture now, a readiness to flee that seems at odds with his profession.

Seven months ago, Marcus was pulled over during a routine drive home from the airport. He'd been working a double shift-a Sydney to Melbourne run followed by a turnaround to Brisbane-and he was tired, his mind still in the cockpit where he'd been managing a hydraulic issue that required his full attention. The officer approached his window aggressively, and within seconds, Marcus found himself yanked from his vehicle, thrown against the hood, and handcuffed. He was accused of a traffic violation he hadn't committed. The entire interaction lasted twelve minutes. He was released without charges, but something fundamental fractured in those twelve minutes.

Marcus describes the moment the officer's hand gripped his arm as the moment his body stopped obeying him. He remembers the shock of it-the assumption of threat, the loss of control. For someone who spends forty hours a week making split-second decisions with hundreds of lives depending on his judgment, the powerlessness was catastrophic. He'd done nothing wrong. He'd cooperated. And none of it mattered.

Since that night, Marcus has called in sick to his airline more than twenty times. He still goes to work some weeks, but the experience of sitting in the captain's seat has fundamentally changed. His hands shake during pre-flight checks. He finds himself hypervigilant about every instrument reading, second-guessing decisions he would have made instantly before. He's terrified of making a mistake-not because he's suddenly less competent, but because he no longer trusts his judgment about anything. If he misread a situation on the ground so completely that he ended up in handcuffs, how can he trust his assessment of weather systems or mechanical anomalies at thirty thousand feet?

The nights are worse. Marcus lies awake replaying the interaction, his heart racing as though the officer's hand is still on his arm. When he does sleep, he dreams of the handcuffs tightening, of being unable to move. He's started drinking more-a glass of wine becomes two, becomes three. It helps him sleep, or at least it makes him unconscious, which feels like the only escape.

His ex-wife calls occasionally, concerned about something his sister mentioned. Marcus deflects. He doesn't know how to explain that he's terrified of driving now, that he sits in traffic scanning mirrors for police vehicles, that he's started taking alternative routes home even though they add forty minutes to his commute. He's a pilot. He's supposed to be the calm one, the professional, the person others trust with their lives.

The divorce finalized two years ago, and they'd maintained a reasonable distance since then. But now Marcus finds himself avoiding even the possibility of running into people he knows. He's withdrawn from his flying club. He stopped going to his nephew's soccer games. The world feels populated by threats he can't anticipate or control, and the shame of this-the knowledge that he's falling apart over something that lasted twelve minutes-only deepens the isolation.

Marcus comes to therapy because his airline's occupational health officer suggested it might help him return to flying. He's not sure it will. He's not sure anything will.
